Method

How packages get approved, held or dropped

The rubric is deliberately biased toward supply-chain integrity: where a package comes from matters as much as what it does.

Verdicts

Adopt
Meets every constraint for the requirement. Approved for use.
Hold
Usable in narrow cases, does not meet every constraint, or the semantics do not match. Requires an exception.
Avoid
Fails a hard constraint: unfixed advisory, no CI provenance, unmaintained, or unacceptable dependency footprint.
Replace
Viable but superseded by a better candidate in the same requirement.

Buckets

Adopted
May be used. The primary choice is listed first.
On hold
Not approved for the requirement, but not prohibited outright.
Dropped
In use today and must be removed by the deadline.
Rejected
Not permitted for this requirement.

Scoring

Scores are a summary, not the decision. A hard failure (unfixed high/critical advisory, no CI publish, unmaintained) caps the verdict regardless of a high score.

  • 30
    Security

    Known advisories, prototype-pollution behaviour, remediation status, scanner visibility.

  • 25
    Release integrity

    CI publishing, OIDC vs long-lived token, SLSA provenance, pinned actions.

  • 20
    Maintenance

    Release recency, open PR age, maintainer count, org ownership.

  • 15
    Fit

    Semantics, TypeScript inference, ESM/CJS, special-object handling, cycles.

  • 10
    Footprint

    Runtime dependencies, install size, license.

80–100 adopt 60–79 hold 0–59 avoid

Symbols

Used across the tables
✓npm
SLSA provenance is attached to the published npm tarball. Verifiable automatically from the registry.
✓release
Provenance and signatures are attached to GitHub release artifacts only. The npm tarball is unattested, so verify that the shipped files match the attested hashes.
—none
No provenance attestation found.
©MIT
Permissive. No obligations beyond attribution.
©MPL-2.0
Weak copyleft. File-level obligations; review before modifying.
©GPL-3.0
Strong copyleft. Usually disqualifying for distribution.
©Proprietary
Proprietary or custom terms. Not open source; requires legal review.

A dual licence is classified by its most permissive arm, because that is the arm you can choose. DOMPurify's MPL-2.0 OR Apache-2.0 therefore reads as permissive.

Build vs buy

0-100 per package

A high score means buying is the better use of time. The score is independent of the security verdict: a vulnerable package can still represent a capability you should buy from a maintained implementation. It assumes the capability is needed at all.

Scope to rebuild 5/5
Intrinsic difficulty 5/5
Commodity 3/5
Integration cost 2/5
70-100 Buy 50-69 Evaluate 0-49 Build

Review cadence

Each requirement sets review_cadence_days. A review is current until 30 days before its next date, due soon inside that window, and overdue afterwards. Decisions carry an expires_at date and move through active, expiring and expired the same way. Overdue and expiring items surface on the overview page.

Configured cadence: Deep merge of nested configuration objects — 180 days; In-app AI assistant chat interface (React) — 90 days; Sanitize untrusted HTML before rendering — 90 days; Graph visualization in a React application — 90 days.

Adding a review

  1. Add the package to data/packages.json if it is new.
  2. Add the review to data/reviews.json. Include at least one evidence item per decision driver.
  3. Classify it in data/decisions.json under exactly one of adopted, hold, rejected or dropped.
  4. Run npm run validate, then npm run build.
  5. Commit the JSON and the regenerated dist/. The commit is the audit entry.
{
  "id": "rev-2027-04-example",
  "package_id": "pkg-example",
  "requirement_id": "req-deep-merge",
  "reviewed_at": "2027-04-18",
  "recommendation": "adopt",
  "risk": "low",
  "score": 90,
  "summary": "One-sentence verdict.",
  "reasoning": ["Why this verdict."],
  "caveats": ["What could bite us."],
  "evidence": [
    { "key": "provenance", "label": "SLSA provenance", "status": "pass", "detail": "…" }
  ]
}

Known limitations

  • Provenance is not a safety proof. It ties a tarball to a commit and a builder; it does not audit the source.
  • Scanner gaps are real. CVE-2026-93753 is absent from package-scoped OSV matching, so npm audit reports zero for an affected deepmerge@4.3.1. Reviews must check advisories by CVE, not only by package.
  • Download counts are a popularity proxy. They include CI traffic and transitive installs.
  • Bus factor is recorded, not solved. Several "adopt" candidates have a single maintainer; the mitigation is small surface area, org ownership and a short review cadence.
  • Static by design. There is no server and no login. Access control is the git repository and the generated output.
